claim: Atat1cKO mice display significantly reduced responses to adhesive tape applied to the back compared to control mice (p<0.05).
source: While control mice made regular attempts to remove the tape, Atat1cKO mice effectively ignored the tape for much of the time, and the total number of responses was significantly lower (p<0.05) (Figure 1a, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data showing quantified responses to tape stimulus, with statistical significance indicated.

claim: Atat1cKO mice responded significantly less to cotton swab stroking of the paw than control mice (p<0.01).
source: Again, Atat1cKO mice responded significantly less (p<0.01) to this stimulus than Atat1Control mice (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data with statistical analysis.

claim: Atat1cKO mice required significantly higher forces to respond to von Frey filaments throughout the tested range (median threshold 0.4g for control vs 1g for Atat1cKO, p=0.003).
source: However, Atat1cKO mice required significantly higher forces to evoke a response throughout the range of von-Frey filaments (median threshold 0.4g for Atat1Control and 1g for Atat1cKO p=0.003, Mann-Whitney test) (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by von Frey filament testing data with statistical analysis.

claim: Atat1cKO mice displayed substantially longer response latencies to a tail clip compared to control mice (p<0.01).
source: Atat1cKO mice displayed substantially longer response latencies to the clip compared to Atat1Control mice and again, essentially ignored this noxious stimulus (p<0.01) (Figure 1d, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data measuring response latency.

claim: There was no difference in withdrawal latencies to noxious heat between Atat1cKO and control mice in the hotplate test.
source: We observed no difference in withdrawal latencies to a range of temperatures in the hotplate test between Atat1cKO and Atat1Control mice (Figure 1e)
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data showing no significant difference.

claim: Sensitivity to cooling of the paw with acetone was comparable in Atat1cKO and control mice.
source: Similarly, sensitivity to cooling of the paw with acetone was comparable in Atat1cKO and Atat1Control mice (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data showing no significant difference.

claim: Atat1cKO and control mice displayed similar latencies to fall from the rotarod across all speeds tested.
source: Atat1cKO and Atat1Control mice displayed similar latencies to fall from the rotating drum across all speeds tested (Figure 1g)
evidence: Supported by motor coordination test data.

claim: Atat1cKO and control mice displayed a similar number of slips from the raised metal grid.
source: and a similar number of slips from the grid (Figure 1h).
evidence: Supported by motor coordination test data.

claim: Atat1 is required for the detection of innocuous and noxious mechanical touch but not for noxious heat or proprioceptive coordination.
source: Thus, Atat1 is required for the detection of innocuous and noxious mechanical touch but not for noxious heat or proprioceptive coordination.
evidence: Inferred from the combined behavioral test results showing selective deficits.

claim: SAM fibers from Atat1cKO mice showed a striking reduction in mechanical sensitivity with reduced action potentials per stimulus.
source: We observed a striking reduction in the mechanical sensitivity of SAM fibres that was apparent as a reduced number of action potentials per stimulus indentation (Figure 2a and b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings from skin-nerve preparation.

claim: SAM fibers from Atat1cKO mice showed a ~10-fold increase in response latency.
source: and a ~10-fold increase in the latency of the response (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) in Atat1cKO mice.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Reductions in SAM fiber firing frequencies were evident during both the ramp phase and static phase of mechanical stimulus.
source: Reductions in firing frequencies were evident during both the ramp phase (Figure 2a) of the mechanical stimulus and during the static phase (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing phase-specific responses.

claim: RAM fibers displayed a reduction in their stimulus response function in Atat1cKO mice.
source: RAM fibres displayed a similar reduction in their stimulus response function (Figure 2c, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: RAM fibers from Atat1cKO mice showed increased latency to the highest displacement stimulus.
source: and an increased latency to the highest displacement stimulus (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: RAM fibers display higher firing frequencies with increasing stimulus speed, a feature which was reduced in Atat1cKO mice.
source: A characteristic of these fibres is that they display higher firing frequencies with increasing stimulus speed (Milenkovic et al., 2008), a feature which was also reduced in Atat1cKO mice (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and citation to previous literature.

claim: D-hairs displayed significant reductions in their stimulus response function in Atat1cKO mice.
source: D-hairs also displayed significant reductions in their stimulus response function (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: D-hairs showed longer latencies for mechanical activation in Atat1cKO mice.
source: as well as longer latencies for mechanical activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: D-hairs showed decreased sensitivity to dynamic stimuli in Atat1cKO mice.
source: and decreased sensitivity to dynamic stimuli (Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 3) in Atat1cKO mice.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Electrical thresholds and conduction velocities were unchanged in low threshold Aβ and Aδ fibers in the absence of Atat1.
source: Electrical thresholds and conduction velocities were unchanged in low threshold Aβ and Aδ fibres in the absence of Atat1 (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Both Aδ-mechanonociceptors and C-fiber mechanonociceptors exhibited a reduced number of action potentials evoked by indentation in the absence of Atat1.
source: Similar to low threshold fibres, both populations of nociceptor exhibited a reduced number of action potentials evoked by indentation (AM units: Figure 3a and b, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Both Aδ-mechanonociceptors and C-fiber mechanonociceptors showed longer latencies for mechanical activation in the absence of Atat1.
source: longer latencies for mechanical activation (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Electrical thresholds and conduction velocities of nociceptors showed no change in the absence of Atat1.
source: and no change in electrical thresholds and conduction velocities in the absence of Atat1 (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Mechanical thresholds to von Frey stimuli were elevated in C-fiber nociceptors from Atat1cKO mice.
source: Mechanical thresholds to von Frey stimuli were also elevated in C-fibre nociceptors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements.

claim: There was no difference between genotypes in the proportion of C-fibers responding to heat, or in their activation thresholds and firing rate in response to heat stimulus.
source: We observed no difference between genotypes in the proportion of C-fibres responding to heat, or in their activation thresholds and firing rate in response to a heat stimulus (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings of heat responses.

claim: Atat1 is specifically required for mechanical sensitivity across all major fiber types innervating the skin.
source: Thus collectively, these data indicate that Atat1 is specifically required for mechanical sensitivity across all major fibre types innervating the skin.
evidence: Inferred from comprehensive electrophysiological analysis of all fiber types.

claim: There was no change in the number of myelinated and unmyelinated fibers in the saphenous nerve upon deletion of Atat1.
source: We observed no change in the number of myelinated and unmyelinated fibres in the saphenous nerve (Figure 4a–d)
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy analysis.

claim: There was no change in the number, density, or organization of terminal endings in the skin upon deletion of Atat1.
source: in the number, density, or organization of terminal endings in the skin (Figure 4e–h)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence analysis of skin innervation.

claim: There was no change in the innervation of the spinal cord by CGRP, IB4 and NF200 positive sensory neurons upon deletion of Atat1.
source: or in the innervation of the spinal cord by CGRP, IB4 and NF200 positive sensory neurons (Figure 4m–p and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence analysis of spinal cord sections.

claim: There was no difference in the growth rate or length of axons in DRG from Atat1Control and Atat1cKO mice in whole mount explants.
source: In whole mount DRG explants supported in the presence of NGF we detected no difference in the growth rate or length of axons in DRG from Atat1Control and Atat1cKO mice (Figure 4i–k).
evidence: Supported by axon outgrowth assay measurements.

claim: The displacement and velocity of quantum dot labelled NGF molecules was not altered in the absence of Atat1.
source: Moreover, single molecule imaging of NGF/receptor transport in a microfluidic device revealed that the displacement and velocity of quantum dot labelled NGF molecules (Sung et al., 2011), was not altered in the absence of Atat1 (Figure 4l, Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Video 3).
evidence: Supported by single molecule tracking experiments and citation to methodology.

claim: The loss of mechanosensitivity does not arise from generalized effects on neuronal function but from defects in the ability of sensory neurons to transduce mechanical forces into electrical signals.
source: Taken together with electrophysiological analysis, these data indicate that the loss of mechanosensitivity is not due to generalized effects on neuronal function but rather arises from defects in the ability of sensory neurons to transduce mechanical forces into electrical signals.
evidence: Inferred from combined morphological and functional analyses showing selective deficits.

claim: In the absence of Atat1, there was a marked loss in the number of mechanically sensitive neurons evoked by cell prodding that was evident across each subtype of current.
source: In the absence of Atat1, we observed a marked loss in the number of mechanically sensitive neurons evoked by cell prodding that was evident across each subtype of current (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by patch clamp recordings from cultured DRG neurons.

claim: The small proportion of neurons which still displayed mechanosensitive currents in Atat1cKO mice exhibited significantly reduced current amplitudes and higher thresholds.
source: Furthermore, the small proportion of neurons which still displayed mechanosensitive currents in Atat1cKO mice exhibited significantly reduced current amplitudes and higher thresholds (Figure 5b–d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by patch clamp recordings.

claim: Mechanosensitive currents in Atat1cKO neurons showed no difference in their activation kinetics.
source: but no difference in their activation kinetics (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by patch clamp recordings.

claim: Voltage gated channel activity, resting membrane potential, action potential threshold, and sensitivity to capsaicin or pH were indistinguishable between Atat1Control and Atat1cKO mice.
source: Other functional parameters such as voltage gated channel activity, resting membrane potential, action potential threshold, and sensitivity to capsaicin or pH were indistinguishable between Atat1Control and Atat1cKO mice (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological and calcium imaging measurements.

claim: There was no difference in Fluorescence Recovery After Bleaching (FRAP) of a Piezo2-GFP fusion construct transfected into dissociated neurons in the absence of Atat1.
source: We also examined perimembrane dynamics of the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo2 in the absence of Atat1, and observed no difference in Fluorescence Recovery After Bleaching (FRAP) of a Piezo2-GFP fusion construct transfected into dissociated neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by FRAP analysis.

claim: The reduced mechanical sensitivity of DRG neurons in Atat1cKO mice does not arise from compromised membrane properties or defects in mechanosensitive ion channel trafficking.
source: Thus the reduced mechanical sensitivity of DRG neurons in Atat1cKO mice does not arise from compromised membrane properties in these cells or defects in mechanosensitive ion channel trafficking.
evidence: Inferred from functional assays showing normal membrane properties and channel trafficking.

claim: Transfection of wild-type Atat1 rescued mechanosensitivity in Atat1cKO cultures and restored the proportion of RA, IA and SA responses to control levels.
source: As a positive control we determined that transfection of an Atat1-YFP construct rescued mechanosensitivity in Atat1cKO cultures and that the proportion of RA, IA and SA responses across the DRG returned to control levels (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by patch clamp recordings from transfected neurons.

claim: Expression of catalytically inactive Atat1 (Atat1-GGL) did not restore mechanosensitivity in Atat1cKO neurons.
source: Expression of Atat1-GGL did not restore mechanosensitivity in Atat1cKO neurons, and we observed no difference in the proportion of different types of mechanically activated current compared to mock EGFP transfection (Figure 5e).
evidence: Supported by patch clamp recordings from transfected neurons.

claim: The acetyltransferase activity of Atat1 is required for normal mechanical sensitivity of DRG neurons.
source: Thus the acetyltransferase activity of Atat1 is required for normal mechanical sensitivity of DRG neurons.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments comparing wild-type and catalytically inactive Atat1.

claim: Expression of K40Q α-tubulin (acetylation mimic) rescued mechanosensitivity of Atat1cKO DRG neurons to control levels.
source: Expression of K40Q α-tubulin rescued mechanosensitivity of Atat1cKO DRG neurons to Atat1Control levels, while a charge conserving control mutation (K40R) had no significant effect (Figure 5f).
evidence: Supported by patch clamp recordings from transfected neurons.

claim: The acetyltransferase activity of Atat1 modulates mechanosensitivity and acetylated α-tubulin is the likely effector.
source: Collectively these data strongly indicate that the acetyltransferase activity of Atat1 modulates mechanosensitivity and that acetylated α-tubulin is the likely effector.
evidence: Inferred from genetic rescue experiments with acetylation mimics.

claim: Microtubules form an interweaved network in all DRG neurons examined, especially towards the centre of the cell.
source: We performed superresolution dSTORM (direct stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy)(microscopy on DRG neurons stained with α-tubulin antibodies, and indeed observed that microtubules form an interweaved network in all neurons examined, especially towards the centre of the cell (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: Supported by superresolution microscopy observations.

claim: There were no clearly visible differences in microtubule organization between Atat1Control and Atat1cKO sensory neurons.
source: However, we were unable to detect clearly visible differences in organization between Atat1Control and Atat1cKO sensory neurons (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: Supported by superresolution microscopy observations.

claim: There was no difference in microtubule density, the number of microtubule crossing points, or the angular variance of the microtubule cytoskeleton between Atat1Control and Atat1cKO mice.
source: We observed no difference in microtubule density (Figure 6g), the number of microtubule crossing points (Figure 6h), or the angular variance of the microtubule cytoskeleton (Figure 6i) in any neuron between Atat1Control and Atat1cKO mice indicating that acetylation does not influence the gross organization of the microtubule network.
evidence: Supported by automated quantitative analysis of superresolution images.

claim: Acetylation does not influence the gross organization of the microtubule network.
source: indicating that acetylation does not influence the gross organization of the microtubule network.
evidence: Inferred from quantitative analysis showing no differences in microtubule organization parameters.

claim: There was no difference in the organization of the actin network upon deletion of Atat1.
source: To investigate whether the absence of microtubule acetylation could indirectly impact upon the actin cytoskeleton, we also performed phalloidin staining on DRG neurons. Again we did not detect any difference in the organization of the actin network upon deletion of Atat1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by phalloidin staining observations.

claim: Acetylated α-tubulin was concentrated in a band directly under the plasma membrane in cultured DRG neurons that was evident in 80 ± 5% of neurons.
source: Strikingly, we observed that acetylated α-tubulin was concentrated in a band directly under the plasma membrane in cultured DRG neurons that was evident in 80 ± 5% of neurons (Figure 7a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence observations with quantification.

claim: Total α-tubulin was distributed evenly across the cytoplasm of all DRG cells.
source: while total α-tubulin was distributed evenly across the cytoplasm of all cells (Figure 7b).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence observations.

claim: The submembrane acetylated α-tubulin band was not present in non-mechanosensory cells such as serum-starved fibroblasts where acetylated α-tubulin was found throughout the microtubule network.
source: Importantly, this band was not present in non-mechanosensory cells such as serum-starved fibroblasts where acetylated α-tubulin was found throughout the microtubule network (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: Supported by comparative immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Acetylation was enriched under the membrane of axons in the saphenous nerve.
source: Acetylation was enriched under the membrane of axons in the saphenous nerve (as determined from staining with a Myelin Basic Protein antibody) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence observations of nerve sections.

claim: Acetylated α-tubulin was apparently present at sensory neuron terminal endings in the cornea where mechanotransduction takes place.
source: and also apparently at sensory neuron terminal endings in the cornea where mechanotransduction takes place (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Video 4).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence observations of cornea preparations.

claim: In the absence of Atat1 and acetylated α-tubulin, the stiffness of sensory neurons was significantly higher across a range of indentations extending from 200 nm to 600 nm (p<0.01).
source: In DRG neurons from Atat1cKO mice we observed that cellular stiffness was significantly higher across a range of indentations extending from displacements of 200 nm to 600 nm (p<0.01) (Figure 7e and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by atomic force microscopy measurements.

claim: Higher forces are required to indent sensory neurons from Atat1cKO mice than Atat1Control mice.
source: Thus higher forces are required to indent sensory neurons from Atat1cKO mice than Atat1Control mice.
evidence: Inferred from AFM measurements showing increased cellular stiffness.

claim: In the absence of Atat1, sensory neuron axons displayed less shrinkage than control counterparts in response to hyperosmotic stimulus.
source: We confirmed this further by assaying the shrinkage of sensory neurons induced by a hyperosmotic stimulus. In the absence of Atat1, sensory neuron axons displayed less shrinkage than their control counterparts, an effect that could be rescued by expression of the acetylation mimicking mutation α-tubulin K40Q (p<0.05) (Figure 7f).
evidence: Supported by osmotic shrinkage assay measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: Expression of α-tubulin K40Q rescued the reduced shrinkage phenotype in Atat1cKO sensory neurons (p<0.05).
source: an effect that could be rescued by expression of the acetylation mimicking mutation α-tubulin K40Q (p<0.05) (Figure 7f).
evidence: Supported by osmotic shrinkage assay measurements with genetic rescue.

claim: In DRG neurons from Atat1cKO mice, there was significantly reduced microtubule displacement upon application of hyperosmotic solutions compared to control and K40Q expressing cells (p<0.05).
source: Strikingly, in DRG neurons from Atat1cKO mice we observed significantly reduced microtubule displacement upon application of hyperosmotic solutions compared to control and K40Q expressing cells (p<0.05) (Figure 7g to m)
evidence: Supported by live imaging of microtubules during osmotic challenge.

claim: In the absence of α-tubulin acetylation, sensory neurons are more resistant to mechanical deformation.
source: again supporting the premise that in the absence of α-tubulin acetylation sensory neurons are more resistant to mechanical deformation.
evidence: Inferred from AFM, osmotic shrinkage, and microtubule compression experiments.

claim: Deletion of the α-tubulin acetyltransferase Atat1 from mouse peripheral sensory neurons results in a profound and remarkably selective loss of cutaneous mechanical sensation.
source: Here we establish that deletion of the α-tubulin acetyltransferase Atat1 from mouse peripheral sensory neurons results in a profound and remarkably selective loss of cutaneous mechanical sensation.
evidence: Supported by comprehensive behavioral and electrophysiological data.

claim: The loss of mechanical sensation impacts strongly upon both light touch and pain.
source: We demonstrate that this impacts strongly upon both light touch and pain
evidence: Supported by behavioral tests showing deficits in both innocuous and noxious mechanical stimuli.

claim: All mechanoreceptor subtypes which innervate the skin are less responsive in the absence of Atat1.
source: and that all mechanoreceptor subtypes which innervate the skin are less responsive in the absence of Atat1.
evidence: Supported by skin-nerve electrophysiology showing reduced responses across all fiber types.

claim: The mechanosensory phenotype arises from reduction of the amplitude of mechanically activated currents in sensory neurons.
source: This phenotype arises from reduction of the amplitude of mechanically activated currents in sensory neurons
evidence: Supported by patch clamp recordings showing reduced current amplitudes.

claim: The mechanosensory phenotype is mediated by the loss of a sub-membrane band of acetylated α-tubulin in Atat1cKO mice that sets mechanical rigidity of these cells.
source: and we propose that it is mediated by the loss of a sub-membrane band of acetylated α-tubulin in Atat1cKO mice that sets mechanical rigidity of these cells.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on observations of acetylated tubulin localization and cellular stiffness measurements.

claim: Cellular stiffness regulates mechanical sensitivity by setting the force required to indent the plasma membrane and activate mechanosensitive ion channels.
source: Our data thus describe a model whereby cellular stiffness regulates mechanical sensitivity by setting the force required to indent the plasma membrane and activate mechanosensitive ion channels.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic model based on the experimental findings.

claim: Acetylated microtubules are likely the effector for the loss of mechanosensation in Atat1cKO mice, suggesting that mammals and nematodes may utilize Atat1 differentially in controlling touch sensation.
source: Thus acetylated microtubules are likely the effector for the loss of mechanosensation in Atat1cKO mice, suggesting that mammals and nematodes may utilize Atat1 differentially in controlling touch sensation.
evidence: Inferred from genetic rescue experiments and comparison with C. elegans literature.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton is an essential component of the mammalian mechanotransduction complex.
source: Our results indicate that the microtubule cytoskeleton is an essential component of the mammalian mechanotransduction complex
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive functional deficits observed upon Atat1 deletion.

claim: By influencing cellular stiffness, α-tubulin acetylation can tune mechanical sensitivity across the full range of mechanoreceptor subtypes.
source: and that by influencing cellular stiffness, α-tubulin acetylation can tune mechanical sensitivity across the full range of mechanoreceptor subtypes.
evidence: Inferred from observations that all mechanoreceptor subtypes are affected and cellular stiffness is altered.

claim: At its most fundamental level, touch sensation requires the translation of mechanical energy into mechanosensitive ion channel opening, thereby generating electro-chemical signals.
source: At its most fundamental level, touch sensation requires the translation of mechanical energy into mechanosensitive ion channel opening, thereby generating electro-chemical signals.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mechanotransduction.

claim: Mechanical forces acting upon cells or tissues are propagated into the opening of mechanically gated ion channels such as Piezo2 as the first step in the sense of touch.
source: Mechanical forces acting upon cells or tissues are propagated into the opening of mechanically gated ion channels such as Piezo2 as the first step in the sense of touch (Abraira and Ginty, 2013; Maksimovic et al., 2014; Ranade et al., 2014; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The bacterial mechanotransduction channel MscS is fully activated by mechanical stimuli when reconstituted in reduced membrane systems.
source: For example, the bacterial mechanotransduction channel MscS (Sukharev, 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Eukaryotic two-pore-domain potassium channels TRAAK and TREK1 are fully activated by mechanical stimuli when reconstituted in reduced membrane systems.
source: and eukaryotic two-pore-domain potassium channels TRAAK and TREK1 (Brohawn et al., 2014a, 2012, 2014b; Lolicato et al., 2014) are fully activated by mechanical stimuli when reconstituted in reduced membrane systems
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1 is likely to be gated by force exerted via lipids due to its exceptional sensitivity to membrane tension.
source: and the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1 is also likely to be gated by force exerted via lipids due to its exceptional sensitivity to membrane tension (Cox et al., 2016; Lewis and Grandl, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In-vivo, membrane ion channels are not isolated from the cytoplasm and extracellular matrix, and mechanical sensitivity may depend on further interaction with other cellular components such as the underlying cytoskeleton to modify and redistribute membrane tension.
source: However, in-vivo, membrane ion channels are not isolated from the cytoplasm and extracellular matrix, and mechanical sensitivity may depend on further interaction with other cellular components such as the underlying cytoskeleton to modify and redistribute membrane tension (Delmas et al., 2011; Krieg et al., 2015; Qi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila, NompC ion channels were shown to be linked between the plasma membrane and microtubules by a tether protein domain in the N-terminus of the channel, and this linkage is essential for mechanosensitivity of the channel.
source: Indeed, in Drosophila, NompC ion channels were shown to be linked between the plasma membrane and microtubules by a tether protein domain in the N-terminus of the channel, and this linkage is essential for mechanosensitivity of the channel (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In C. elegans, touch sensitivity of specialized touch receptor neurons is dependent on both the actin binding protein β spectrin and the microtubule cytoskeleton.
source: Moreover, in C. elegans touch sensitivity of specialized touch receptor neurons is dependent on both the actin binding protein β spectrin (Krieg et al., 2014) and the microtubule cytoskeleton (Bounoutas et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: C. elegans touch receptor neuron axons are filled with specialized cross-linked bundles of heavily acetylated 15-protofilament microtubules.
source: A feature of C. elegans touch receptor neurons is that their axons are filled with specialized cross-linked bundles of heavily acetylated 15-protofilament microtubules (Chalfie and Thomson, 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of MEC7 β-tubulin and MEC12 α-tubulin leads to a loss of mechanical sensitivity in C. elegans.
source: Disruption of the molecular components of these microtubules, MEC7 β-tubulin and MEC12 α-tubulin leads to a loss of mechanical sensitivity (Bounoutas et al., 2009; Fukushige et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mutation of MEC17, the major tubulin acetyltransferase, reduces touch sensitivity in C. elegans.
source: Moreover, mutation of MEC17, the major tubulin acetyltransferase (Akella et al., 2010; Shida et al., 2010) also reduces touch sensitivity in C. elegans (Cueva et al., 2012; Topalidou et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It is not clear whether the loss of touch sensitivity in MEC17 mutants stems from the absence of tubulin acetylation or from other unknown actions of MEC17.
source: Of note, it is not clear whether this loss of touch sensitivity stems from the absence of tubulin acetylation in MEC17 mutants (Shida et al., 2010) or from other unknown actions of MEC17 (Akella et al., 2010; Davenport et al., 2014; Fukushige et al., 1999; Topalidou et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature showing conflicting findings.

claim: MEC17 functions to transfer an acetyl group to the lysine 40 (K40) residue on the luminal side of microtubules.
source: MEC17 functions to transfer an acetyl group to the lysine 40 (K40) residue on the luminal side of microtubules (Szyk et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The post-translational modification of α-tubulin acetylation at K40 is remarkably well conserved in organisms that have cells with cilia.
source: and this post-translation modification is remarkably well conserved in organisms that have cells with cilia (Shida et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Atat1, the mammalian orthologue of MEC17, is expressed ubiquitously in all mouse peripheral sensory neurons.
source: Intriguingly, Atat1, the mammalian orthologue of MEC17, is expressed ubiquitously in all mouse peripheral sensory neurons (Kalebic et al., 2013a)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mouse peripheral sensory neurons have amongst the highest level of α-tubulin acetylation in the mouse.
source: and these neurons have amongst the highest level of α-tubulin acetylation in the mouse (Kalebic et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Atat1fl/+ mice were crossed with a sensory neuron specific Cre driver line Avil-Cre to generate Atat1cKO and control mice.
source: Atat1fl/+ mice (Kalebic et al., 2013b) were crossed with a sensory neuron specific Cre driver line Avil-Cre (Zurborg et al., 2011) to generate Avil-Cre::Atat1fl/fl (referred to as Atat1cKO) and control Avil-Cre::Atat1fl/+ mice (referred to as Atat1Control).
evidence: Describes the experimental design with citations to mouse line sources.

claim: Avil-Cre mediated deletion is efficient and Cre expression has no apparent effect on sensory driven behaviour.
source: Thus in line with previous reports Avil-Cre mediated deletion is efficient and Cre expression has no apparent effect on sensory driven behaviour (Zurborg et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by comparison with wildtype and full knockout mice, and citation to previous literature.

claim: Sensory neuron axons terminate in the skin and form a diverse range of functionally distinct mechanoreceptors that underlie the sense of touch.
source: Sensory neuron axons terminate in the skin and form a diverse range of functionally distinct mechanoreceptors that underlie the sense of touch (Abraira and Ginty, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mechanoreceptors can be classified by their conduction velocity (into Aβ, Aδ and C fibres), their adaptation properties (into rapidly adapting or slowly adapting) and by their mechanical thresholds (into mechanoreceptors and mechanonociceptors).
source: They can be classified by their conduction velocity (into Aβ, Aδ and C fibres), their adaptation properties (into rapidly adapting or slowly adapting) and by their mechanical thresholds (into mechanoreceptors and mechanonociceptors).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mechanoreceptor classification.

claim: RAM fibers display higher firing frequencies with increasing stimulus speed.
source: A characteristic of these fibres is that they display higher firing frequencies with increasing stimulus speed (Milenkovic et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Mechanically gated currents can be evoked in ~90% of DRG neurons by indentation with a blunt glass probe.
source: Such a stimulus can evoke mechanically gated currents in ~90% of DRG neurons that are further classified as rapidly adapting (RA), intermediate-adapting (IA) and slowly adapting (SA) responses (Hu and Lewin, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The mechanosensitivity of hypothalamic osmosensory neurons is dependent upon a unique interweaved organization of microtubules in these cells.
source: A recent study has demonstrated that the mechanosensitivity of hypothalamic osmosensory neurons is dependent upon a unique interweaved organization of microtubules in these cells (Prager-Khoutorsky et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In C. elegans, several reports indicate that acetylated tubulin is not required for touch sensitivity.
source: Indeed in C. elegans, several reports indicate that acetylated tubulin is not required for touch sensitivity (Akella et al., 2010; Davenport et al., 2014; Fukushige et al., 1999; Topalidou et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It is unknown how MEC17 regulates mechanosensation in C. elegans nematodes.
source: and as such it is unknown as to how MEC17 (the C. elegans orthologue of Atat1) regulates mechanosensation in nematodes.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Atat1 has been shown to have functions beyond its acetyltransferase activity at α-tubulin.
source: In addition to its well characterized role as an α-tubulin acetyltransferase, Atat1 has been shown to have functions beyond its acetyltransferase activity at α-tubulin (Castro-Castro et al., 2012; Kalebic et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Acetylated microtubules depend on microtubules for axonal transport.
source: Given the multitude of cellular processes that depend on microtubules, especially in cells with elongated axons such as peripheral sensory neurons, one possible mechanism by which Atat1 might be affecting mechanosensitivity is via altered structure of the peripheral nervous system, perhaps as a result of aberrant axonal transport in the absence of acetylated microtubules (Reed et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from discussion of potential mechanisms and citation to previous literature on axonal transport.

claim: STOML3 associates with microtubules in a specialized vesicle where it interacts with ASIC subunits.
source: We have previously reported that STOML3, another critical mediator of mechanotransduction, associates with microtubules in a specialized vesicle where it interacts with acid-sensing (proton-gated) ion channel (ASIC) subunits (Lapatsina et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Uncoupling of vesicles from microtubules leads to incorporation of STOML3 into the plasma membrane and increased acid-gated currents.
source: Uncoupling of vesicles from microtubules leads to incorporation of STOML3 into the plasma membrane and increased acid-gated currents.
evidence: This is established from previous work.

claim: Full Atat1 knockout mice display no alterations in proprioception.
source: The lack of proprioceptive phenotype in Atat1cKO mice does not stem from incomplete recombination by the Avil-Cre driver in proprioceptive neurons because we previously observed that full Atat1 knockout mice also display no alterations in proprioception (Kalebic et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Piezo2 knockout mice display severe proprioceptive defects.
source: This is in contrast to Piezo2 knockout mice which display severe proprioceptive defects (Woo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Microtubules have been implicated in sensory mechanotransduction in Drosophila larval dendritic arborisation neurons.
source: For example, microtubules have been implicated in sensory mechanotransduction in Drosophila larval dendritic arborisation neurons (Zhang et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Microtubules have been implicated in sensory mechanotransduction in C. elegans touch receptor neurons.
source: C. elegans touch receptor neurons (Bounoutas et al., 2009; Fukushige et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Microtubules have been implicated in sensory mechanotransduction in mammalian osmosensory neurons.
source: and mammalian osmosensory neurons (Prager-Khoutorsky et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A physical tether has been described in sensory neurons that may link mechanosensitive ion channels to the extracellular matrix.
source: Further support for a tethered mechanotransduction complex comes from observations in sensory neurons where a physical tether has been described that may link mechanosensitive ion channels to the extracellular matrix (Chiang et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: STOML3 has been demonstrated to change the force distribution in neuronal membrane via binding cholesterol.
source: Finally, another critical component of the complex, STOML3 has been demonstrated to change the force distribution in neuronal membrane via binding cholesterol.
evidence: This is established from previous work.

claim: A specific reduction of stiffness in sensory neuron membranes is observed in STOML3 knockout mice.
source: However, while a specific reduction of stiffness in sensory neuron membranes is observed in STOML3 knockout mice (Qi et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Both STOML3 knockout mice and Atat1cKO mice exhibit deficits in mechanosensation despite opposite effects on cellular stiffness.
source: yet both STOML3 knockout mice and Atat1cKO mice exhibit deficits in mechanosensation.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of phenotypes.

claim: Disruption of α-tubulin acetylation increases the overall neuronal stiffness, rendering sensory neurons more resistant to mechanical deformation.
source: One explanation for this difference is that disruption of α-tubulin acetylation increases the overall neuronal stiffness, rendering sensory neurons more resistant to mechanical deformation, and thereby impeding the transmission of force to other mechanical transducing elements, including STOML3, the cytoskeleton, extracellular matrix and plasma membrane.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the experimental findings.

claim: STOML3 distributes force directly within the membrane to ion channels, and a stiffened membrane facilitates this process.
source: In contrast, STOML3 distributes the force directly within the membrane to ion channels, and a stiffened membrane facilitates this process.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on previous knowledge and current findings.

claim: Membrane stiffness may be set at an optimal range to distribute force among the membrane, cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix and thus tune the sensitivity of mechanosensitive ion channels.
source: It is also possible that membrane stiffness is set at an optimal range to distribute force among the membrane, cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix and thus tune the sensitivity of mechanosensitive ion channels.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: Another tubulin posttranslation modification, detyrosination, stiffens cardiomyocytes and promotes microtubule buckling in these cells.
source: Intriguingly, it has recently been shown that another tubulin posttranslation modification, detyrosination, stiffens cardiomyocytes and promotes microtubule buckling in these cells (Robison et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Desmin intermediate filaments were identified as a physical link between detyrosinated microtubules and the sarcomere in cardiomyocytes.
source: Desmin intermediate filaments were identified as a physical link between detyrosinated microtubules and the sarcomere
evidence: This is established from previous work.

claim: The lack of mechanosensitivity of Atat1cKO mice extends beyond phenotypes observed when other mechanotransduction complex proteins such as Piezo2 and STOML3 are deleted.
source: What is clear however is that the mechanism appears to be broadly applicable since the lack of mechanosensitivity of Atat1cKO mice extends beyond phenotypes observed when other mechanotransduction complex proteins such as Piezo2 (Ranade et al., 2014) and STOML3 (Wetzel et al., 2007) are deleted.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with other knockout phenotypes cited in the literature.

claim: The convergence of multiple mechanisms onto a single posttranslational modification of α-tubulin indicates that microtubule acetylation represents a fundamental component of the mechanosensory apparatus.
source: The convergence of multiple mechanisms onto a single posttranslational modification of α-tubulin, and its remarkable selectivity, indicates that microtubule acetylation represents a fundamental component of the mechanosensory apparatus
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comprehensive findings.

claim: Microtubule acetylation represents an attractive target for novel therapeutic strategies to treat mechanical pain.
source: as well as an attractive target for novel therapeutic strategies to treat mechanical pain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications.
